text: The service desk practice exists to capture demand for incident resolution and service requests. ITIL 4 describes it as the entry point and single point of contact for the service provider with all of its users — not a phone queue, not a specific tool, but the one place users go, however they reach it.

Everything else in this chapter flows through that single point of contact in one direction or another — service requests, knowledge articles, SLA performance, and incidents from chapter four all pass through here before anything else happens.

ITIL 4 deliberately broadens the service desk beyond the image of a phone bank. A modern service desk may take contact through a self-service portal, live chat, email, a dedicated phone line, walk-up support, and increasingly AI-driven chatbots that triage a request before a human ever sees it.

None of these channels is the real service desk — they're all valid front doors to the same single point of contact. What matters is that wherever a user starts, their request ends up logged, categorized, and routed the same way, with nothing falling through the cracks.

ITIL 4 is explicit that the service desk's value isn't really about ticket count. It's empathy — understanding how disruptive a problem is for the person reporting it — paired with clear communication and fast, accurate triage: incident or request, how urgent, and which team should own it.

The service desk is the hub this whole chapter runs through — the first classification point, a major source of recurring questions for knowledge management, and where SLA breaches first become visible to a frustrated user. Next up: chapter six opens with service configuration management.
